title: Devarim: small and great alike (Deuteronomy 1:17)
hookLine: judges must hear the small as the great and fear no one

lines: THE BIG FILE AND THE SMALL ONE.
cards: A desk at a city office, two people in line. One is a well-known developer with a lawyer at his elbow and a building permit worth millions.
The other is a retired woman whose neighbor's tree keeps dropping branches on her car. Whose file gets opened first? Whose gets read carefully?
It isn't hard to guess how it often goes. Early in his farewell, Moses remembers setting up courts in the wilderness, and the charge he gave the judges. It's about exactly that line at that desk.

teach.h: HEAR THE SMALL AND THE GREAT ALIKE.
teach.b: The charge, in the old Jewish translation, says: "ye shall hear the small and the great alike; ye shall not be afraid of the face of any man; for the judgment is God's." Three pieces. First, small and great alike.
The rabbis took that literally, about money.

teach.h: A PENNY CASE, A FORTUNE CASE.
teach.b: In the Talmud, in Sanhedrin, Resh Lakish says a case over a single perutah, a tiny copper coin, must be as precious to the judge as a case over a hundred maneh, a fortune. Same care. Same patience.

Second, don't be afraid of the face of any man. A judge will someday face someone powerful, someone who could ruin them, someone with friends. The verse says: don't look away from the case to look at the face.
And the reason is the third piece: the judgment is God's. Read that way, the judge isn't the owner of justice, just the one holding it for a while, and answerable for how it was held.
Notice who is listening to this speech. Not judges, mostly. A whole people.

Moses is retelling it to everyone, because everyone ends up judging something: whose complaint gets heard at work, which kid's version of the fight gets believed, whose message gets answered tonight and whose waits a week.
The small and the great show up at all of those desks.

how: Jewish law holds judges to equal care for every case regardless of its value or the parties' standing, and the Talmud's rule that a penny case is as precious as a fortune is still cited in teaching about Jewish courts.

games.q: inside the judges' charge — tap the pairs.

s: the Talmud says a tiny case deserves less care than a big one
a case over one perutah must be as precious as a case over a hundred maneh.
Moses tells the judges not to be afraid of anyone
"ye shall not be afraid of the face of any man."
Moses gives this charge only to judges, in private
in Deuteronomy he retells it to the whole people.

games.q: you're a judge. one case is over a single copper coin, the other over a fortune, and the rich man is impatient. what does the Talmud say?
o: hear the fortune first; it matters more.
settle the coin case quickly to clear the docket.
treat the coin case as precious as the fortune.
games.why: Sanhedrin reads small and great alike as a penny case being as precious as a case over a hundred maneh.

practice: Bring to mind a small worry someone brought you lately that you brushed past: a kid's question, a coworker's minor complaint, a parent's repeated story.
Hold it up the way you'd hold a big one, and ask what they were really asking for. Let yourself feel the size it was to them.

wordCard.voice: Devarim. Words, the name of this last book, where Moses retells even the charge he gave the first judges.

orig.note: Hebrew: as the small, as the great. the judges' charge in Deuteronomy 1:17.

carryVoice: Your line: small and great alike. A week of edges: a date remembered, a city of refuge, a land that's shared, the edge of the Jordan, and now the words. That's day four hundred eighty-three.
